summary: This is an April 1st humor RFC, so it should not be read as a real specification. It jokes about routers and middleboxes that terminate IP packets, presenting common scenarios of 'wrongful termination' and recommendations for avoiding them. The text plays on legal language about unfair dismissal.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke paper that pretends packets can be unfairly fired from their jobs by routers. It is meant to make network people laugh.

subtitle: Discrimination against IP packets by routers and middleboxes

tldr.problem: Routers and middleboxes sometimes drop packets based on characteristics like age, color, origin, length, or version, which constitutes unfair discrimination.
tldr.mechanism: This April 1st RFC humorously frames packet filtering as employment discrimination, recommending that devices become 'Equal Opportunity Devices' that respect all packets regardless of their attributes.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st humor document. It uses employment law terminology to discuss networking concepts while highlighting real behaviors that engineers sometimes debate.

today: RFC 8367 is an April 1st humor document published in the Independent Submission stream. While written as a joke, it highlights real networking behaviors that engineers sometimes debate. The document is informational and should not be treated as policy guidance.

sections.title: The Premise
sections.content:
This is an April 1st humor RFC that uses employment law language to discuss packet filtering. It frames various common router behaviors as discriminatory practices and recommends that routers become 'Equal Opportunity Devices.'

The RFC humorously compares packet characteristics like TTL (age), color (from metering), source address prefix (origin), size (length), IP version, and fragmentation flags to protected characteristics in employment discrimination law.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone wrote a funny paper pretending that routers are employers and packets are job applicants who get wrongfully fired.

sections.title: Types of Wrongful Termination
sections.content:
Color-Based Termination: Metering mechanisms in routers often use packet color (green, yellow, or red from RFC 4115) to decide which packets to discard. The RFC jokingly recommends 'color-blind metering' for equal opportunity.

Age-Based Termination: Routers drop packets with TTL or Hop Limit of 0 or 1, called 'senior packets.' The RFC proposes 'reverse discrimination' in favor of senior packets for control-plane protocols like traceroute.

Origin-Based Termination: Source IP filtering based on address prefix is called 'origin-based filtering.' The RFC jokes that punishing an entire autonomous system for one bad host is unfair.

Length-Based Termination: Short IP packets (under 46 octets) are dropped to meet Ethernet frame size minimums. The RFC recommends not discriminating based on packet length.

IP-Version-Based Termination: Some networks reject IPv6 packets. The RFC sarcastically notes it is 'unsettling' that IPv6 still gets dropped in the 21st century.

Flag-Based Termination: Fragmented packets (with the More Fragments flag set) are often discarded. The RFC recommends respecting all flags.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers drop packets for different reasons: color, age, where it came from, how big it is, what version it is, or what flags it has. The funny paper says this is unfair.

sections.title: The Outcome
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that every router should be an 'Equal Opportunity Device that does not discriminate on the basis of actual or perceived rate, color, age, origin, length, IP version, fragmentation characteristics, higher-layer protocols, or any other IP characteristic.'

The Security Considerations section notes that a liberal approach to packet filtering may compromise security, but argues that 'security must be seen to be done.' This is ironic: while the RFC humorously argues against filtering, real networks need filtering for security.
sections.plainLanguage: The funny ending says routers should treat all packets fairly, no matter what they are.
